title: TA9-17592
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXX XXXXX ("the claimant" or XXX), a 19 year-old citizen of St. Lucia, claims refugee protection pursuant to both sections 96 and 97(1)(b) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act (IRPA).1 The claimant also claims "undue hardship".

This claim had been joined to that of her sister, XXXX XXXXX,2 pursuant to Rule 49 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules,3 and they appeared together for their joint hearing on 20 January 2011. Although the claimants were sisters and each alleged that they required Canada's protection from ex-boyfriends, the similarity of their claims ended there. The claimants each feared a different agent of persecution, each came to Canada at different times and at least one sister had travelled abroad before coming to Canada.

I separated the two sisters' claims through a combination of Rules 50 and 69 as I was of the opinion that separating the claims would better promote the efficient administration of the Division. Allegations

The claimant alleged, in her Personal Information Form (PIF)4 narrative, that her mom and dad left her with her sister (XXXX) in Saint Lucia at age 9. The claimant has two sisters, XXXX and XXXX. XXXX moved to the United Kingdom with her parents and is either the eldest child5 or the middle child.6 When XXX was 14 in 2006, her sister-guardian left for Canada and XXX decided to move in with her boyfriend.
In 2008, XXX travelled to England to meet an internet friend and search for her parents. She remained in the United Kingdom for six months and returned to Saint Lucia.
After she returned, her boyfriend became abusive, controlling and jealous. He destroyed her original St. Lucian passport.
Someone knocked her unconscious one night but she suspects it was her boyfriend. Fearing he might kill her, she left him and then came to Canada. Determination
In making my determination with respect to the claimant, I considered and attempted to apply the Gender Guidelines.7

I find that the claimant has not satisfied her burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, or that she would personally be subjected, on a balance of probabilities, to a danger of torture, or a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment upon return to her country. Therefore, I find that the claimant is not a Convention refugee and is not a person in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA. Analysis

Credibility and subjective fear emerged as the determinative issues in this claim. In arriving at my decision, I considered the claimant's seeming lack of subjective fear, her initial lack of documents, the arrival of subsequent documents and how that impacted on her credibility. Identity

The identity of the claimant as a national of St. Lucia is established by the claimant's testimony and the supporting documentation filed, namely the passport found in Exhibit R/A-2. However, whether the claimant has status in the United Kingdom has not been established nor ruled out by the panel. Please see below, under credibility. Credibility

In order to be determined to be either a Convention refugee or a person in need of protection, the evidence must establish that the claimant would face a serious possibility of persecution for a Convention ground or must establish that his or her removal to the country of nationality would subject him or her, personally, either, (a) to a danger, believed on substantial grounds to exist, of torture within the meaning of Article 1 of the Convention Against Torture; or (b) to a risk to their life or to a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment.

The standard of proof to be applied in assessing whether the claimant has good grounds for fearing persecution for at least one of the grounds in the Convention refugee definition is set out in Adjei.8 In assessing the credibility of the evidence presented by the claimant, I am mindful of the decision of the Federal Court of Appeal in Maldonado9 wherein the Court stated, in part, that "when a claimant swears to the truth of certain allegations, this creates a presumption that those allegations are true unless there be reason to doubt their truthfulness". I also considered the principle established by the Federal Court of Appeal in Dan-Ash,10 that such presumption of truthfulness may be rebutted by the existence of contradictions in the evidence presented by the claimant and that it is a valid basis for a finding of lack of credibility.

The evaluation of the credibility and probative value of the evidence must be made with regard to the totality of the evidence, including what is generally known about the conditions and laws of the country the claimant is from,11 as well as the experiences of similarly situated persons in that country.12 In assessing the claimant's credibility, I have also considered the decision in Orelien13 wherein the Federal Court of Appeal held that it is necessary for the claimant to establish that his or her evidence is probably credible or trustworthy, not just possibly so. I took into consideration the various factors that could affect the claimant's testimony including her young age, cultural differences, testimony given through the filter of an interpreter and hearing-room anxiety.14 "The 'presumption' that a claimant's sworn testimony is true is always rebuttable, and, in appropriate circumstances, may be rebutted by the failure of the documentary evidence to mention what one would normally expect it to mention."15

While it is possible that the claimant's story is true, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that it is not. In arriving at this finding, I am guided by the provision of Section 106 of the Act and Rule 7 of the Refugee Protection Division Rules,16 which impose a duty on the claimant to provide acceptable documents establishing the claimant's identity and other elements of the claim, in the case at hand, her alleged agent of harm, or to provide a satisfactory explanation for a lack thereof. There was nothing to link the claimant to the documentary evidence.

For example, the claimant's story regarding her travel to the United Kingdom does not make any sense. She stated that she met a person on the internet and went to visit her in England. Although not mentioned in her PIF narrative, the claimant testified that this woman paid for her airfare. I could only speculate as to why an internet stranger would pay an airfare for a 16 year-old girl as the claimant was not forthcoming with any rationale for the free trip, other than this person felt sorry for her.

At the time of her first hearing, before I separated the claim from that of her sister, the claimant had no documents, other than the brand new passport seized by the Minister of Citizenship and Immigration (CIC) when she made her claim. She testified that she had an older passport on which she travelled to and from the United Kingdom but her ex-boyfriend burned it. There is no reason for me to accept this allegation. From my experience both as a member of this Division and in my professional life before becoming a member, I gained some experience with passports. The passport disclosed by CIC has no notation or other indication that this passport is a replacement passport for one destroyed before it expired. Furthermore, the claimant, to obtain a replacement passport, would need to file a police report and provide that report to the passport issuing office in Saint Lucia. The claimant did not disclose any such report. This passport was issued in Saint Lucia in XXXX 2009, just before the claimant came to Canada. I find it more likely than not that the claimant travelled to the United Kingdom and possibly back to Saint Lucia on a passport that she has not disclosed that contains information that she does not want me to know. It is possible that the claimant travelled to the United Kingdom on her mother's passport but then the claimant would need her own passport to travel back to Saint Lucia, unless she returned to Saint Lucia on her mother's passport when she was a minor. This would mean that the claimant left Saint Lucia in 2000 or earlier when she was about 9. It is also possible that the claimant obtained status in theUnited Kingdom and travelled to Saint Lucia on a British passport.

In either event, I find17 that the claimant's story is not true. Instead, I believe it more plausible that XXX left Saint Lucia with her parents and the middle child XXXX, leaving the eldest child alone in Saint Lucia, rather than the story XXX wants the Division to accept, that is her parents left the claimant, the youngest child of her parents, in Saint Lucia with XXXX, the eldest child.

When one looks at the allegations - a lost or destroyed passport, a sojourn in the United Kingdom where her parents live, a missing sister who may also be in the United Kingdom, another sister in Canada who allegedly raised her, a generous internet friend, the failure in locating her parents, the claimant's return to Saint Lucia - there are at least two possibilities regarding the claimant's sojourn in the United Kingdom. Either the claimant's allegations are true - she travelled to and lived in England at the expense of an internet "pen pal" or the claimant's allegations are false - she left Saint Lucia with her parents and older sister, XXXX, and lived there from the age of 9 until she came to Canada via Saint Lucia in 2009.

The burden of proof with respect to a claim rests on the claimant. Facts in issue must be proven by the party with the onus on a balance of probabilities. The evidence provided must always be clear, convincing and cogent to satisfy the balance of probabilities test [F.H. v. McDougall, 2008 SCC 53 (CanLII)]. Mr Justice Rothstein, writing for the majority, agreed at paragraph 44 with Lord Hoffman in the case of In re B at paragraph 2: If a legal rule requires a fact to be proved (a fact "in issue"), a judge or jury must decide whether or not it happened. There is no room for a finding that it might have happened. The law operates a binary system in which the only values are zero and one. The fact either happened or it did not. If the tribunal is left in doubt, the doubt is resolved by a rule that one party or the other carries the burden of proof. If the party who bears the burden of proof fails to discharge it, a value of zero is returned and the fact is treated as not having happened. If he does discharge it, a value of one is returned and the fact is treated as having happened.

It is possible that XXX's parents left her at age 9 with her middle sister XXXX and took her eldest sister XXXX with them to the United Kingdom. It is also possible that someone she met on the internet sprang for her return airfare, provided her free room and board for six months and drove her from London to Liverpool to search for her parents. It is possible, too, that, after returning to Saint Lucia, her boyfriend became jealous, controlling and abusive to the point he beat her and burned her passport. However, the claimant has not established any of these facts on a balance of probabilities and has not provided any information as to what she did in London for six months, other than she went once to look for her mother in Liverpool.

With respect to the internet acquaintance, the claimant provided a page of text18 that may or may not have been sent to the claimant by electronic mail from one XXXX XXXXX. XXX failed to name her internet benefactor in her PIF narrative or to CIC in her claim for protection. The item in Exhibit C-3 ostensibly from "XXXX XXXXX" is not in a recognized email form. The correspondent alleged that XXX is a Christian she has known for five years since meeting XXX via a social networking site. There is no evidence which social networking site the correspondent is referring to and there is no other example of their correspondence than the letter in support of her refugee claim, nor is there any copy of the social networking intercourse. The content of the letter disclosed, although it corroborates the testimony of the claimant, makes as little sense as the testimony. If XXX wanted to find her parents, she and XXXX did precious little to accomplish that goal. XXXX drove XXX to an address in Liverpool where her parents allegedly lived at some point but they could not find them. They checked with the inhabitants and neighbours but no one knew where they had gone, or when and some had never heard of them. Neither XXX nor XXXX did anything else to locate her parents that we know about - they did not advertise in the newspapers, they did not go to the police or British immigration authorities, they did not visit any Liverpool churches - they did nothing as far as I can tell other than make one fruitless stab at finding them by going to an old address.

Instead of speculating why XXX would accept free passage to London to live with an internet stranger when all she had was an old address from her mother or why Ms. XXXXX would pay for XXX to do so for six months, I find that it is more likely than not that XXX either left Saint Lucia with her parents and her sister XXXX or she knew all along where they were and visited them in England. I find also that it is less likely that XXX' boyfriend destroyed an earlier St. Lucian passport than she obtained an original St. Lucian passport in 2009. The reason for this finding is that the passport in evidence is a newly-issued passport without any indication that it replaced a passport issued earlier. This suggests to this panel (and I so find) that the claimant likely has or had status in the United Kingdom. I note that the claimant failed to provide her British immigration file, which would have cleared up this mystery. As a result of these findings, I find that the story about her trip to and sojourn in the United Kingdom is not credible.

Also, I find that the claimant failed to establish the identity of the person whom she says she fears, her unnamed conjugal partner. There is no evidence before the Board, except what the claimant wrote and said, as to who he is. In fact, the claimant fails to mention her agent of harm by name in her PIF, or in the Port of Entry notes. I find that it would have been not unreasonable to expect that the claimant could find, if the agent of harm is a person of power or influence, some documentation about him and who, therefore, could be a serious threat to her. Furthermore, it seems to be too convenient that this "conjugal partner" would not be a problem for the claimant before she left but become so after her return.

The claimant also has not been consistent with her dates. At one point the claimant indicates that she travelled to the United Kingdom until XXXX 2008 and then "... after two years,..." (which would be in 2010) her boyfriend began to abuse her. However, the claimant came to Canada in 2009, which would be prior to any problem from him.

The claimant's testimony was marked with inconsistencies, contradictions and implausibilities. The claimant's evidence concerning the more material aspects of her claim was neither consistent nor cogent. Given the importance of the search for her parents to her story, it is reasonable to expect the claimant to give clear and consistent evidence in this regard. She did not.

For all these reasons, I find that there is no trustworthy or credible evidence for the claimant's alleged fear, whether under section 96 or section 97 of the Act. Accordingly, I reject the claim of XXX XXXX. (signed) 'James V. Railton' James V. The panel is aware that the claimant has the burden to establish his claim with "clear, cogent and convincing evidence", which does not raise the standard of proof but merely indicates that a panel must be satisfied the facts in issue are more likely than not to have occurred. Should the panel not be able to determine if a fact in issue is established by the claimant, when it is his burden to do so, then the panel will find the fact has not been established. On the other hand, the panel is aware that, once the facts respecting an allegation of persecution is found, then the panel must determine if, on those facts, there is more than a mere possibility of persecution in the future, that is to say, a "reasonable chance" of persecution for a Convention ground, as set out in Adjei. 18 Exhibit C-3 received 17 March 2011 --------------- ------------------------------------------------------------ --------------- ------------------------------------------------------------ RPD.15.7 (February 12, 2009) Disponible en français RPD.15.7 (February 12, 2009) Disponible en français RPD File No. : TA9-17592 RPD File No. :TA9-17592
